fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "The Three Fire Signs and Why Dylan Wanted This Recording", "body": "Dylan Saccoccio opens with a formal introduction, framing the three voices as the fire signs of the zodiac, Chance as Aries, himself as Leo and Crrow777 as Sagittarius, and reading the recording date of 6/6/24 as the sun's number before quoting Ezekiel 10:9 through 11 on the creeping things and idols graved on the walls. He credits Chance and Crrow777 with the motivation to publish books four through six of his Spirit World series, points listeners to crrow777radio.com and the award winning documentary Shoot the Moon made with Jason Lindgren, and calls Crow a warrior in a garden."}, {"title": "Relocating the Second Sun on 6/6/24", "body": "Crrow777 says that two days before the recording he relocated what he calls the sun we do not see, filmed in Michigan with a technical advisor whose systems produce six gigabyte clips from a 2000 frame capture. He describes first finding it around 2014 and again in 2015 through a Coronado 90mm Solar Max in the hydrogen alpha spectrum at roughly 5 AU, blocking the objective with his hand and a four foot cardboard tube to rule out lens flare, and cites Chris Van Metre reproducing it and an SLU Observatory clip. He stresses that his reading of the sunset spraying is speculation."}, {"title": "Movies, Music and the Social Engineering Apparatus", "body": "The conversation turns to what Crrow777 calls a social engineering apparatus. He argues 2001: A Space Odyssey was high budget and built to make the world accept that we were about to go to the moon, notes the soliloquy at the end of the sequel 2010 about children growing up under two suns, and objects to Dune putting five races into the Fremen when the story required a single ancient people tied to nature. He praises the Japanese film The Burmese Harp as story driven, criticises Pink Floyd tribute acts for regurgitating old art, and says genres with no melody or harmony should be called poetry to a beat."}, {"title": "Symbolic Literacy, Hypocrites and the Priesthood in Theater", "body": "Chance Garton offers symbolic literacy as psychic self-defense, arguing that nobody is fully immune to the hooks of manipulative media but that reading the symbolism lets you see where the Overton window is being shifted and sound the alarm. That sets up the Reverend Robert Taylor deep dive on the origins of the priesthood in theater and the story of Lazarus: the first actors were called hypocrites, they were priests performing tragedies, they could not be buried in the same graveyard as Christians and it was against the law for them to hold office because nobody could tell when they were acting."}, {"title": "The Lunar Wave, Deplatforming and the Cost of the Work", "body": "Crrow777 walks through the footage he calls the lunar wave, first shot in 2012, almost deleted as a camera glitch and pulled back out of his trash after a late night realisation, then filmed a second time roughly a year and a half later. He argues two waves offset the image of the moon, says firmament wave would be the better name, and notes captures in front of Jupiter and Saturn. He ties his deplatforming to calling the Mandalay Bay shooting staged against the opening of Macbeth, and reports losing a channel, tens of thousands of subscribers and search returns that fell from millions to about a thousand."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: Inner Whirled 5 welcomes Crrow777 to the show for the first time. Chance, Dylan Saccoccio and astronomer-researcher Crrow777 dig into Reverend Robert Taylor's astronomico-theological lectures and the deeper meaning behind one of the most striking stories in the New Testament, the raising of Lazarus.
fields.Intro Paragraph 2: In this session: Crrow's catalyst role in connecting researchers and bringing this work to wider audiences, his major astronomical discoveries including the lunar wave and his observations of the sun, the philosophy of belief versus knowing, the cost of building independent platforms after YouTube censorship, a preview of his documentary Shoot The Moon, and the framework that sets up Reverend Robert Taylor's eviscerating critique of why belief is not the safe side.

fields.Plus Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "Belief Is Not The Safe Side", "body": "Chance opens the second hour by putting Taylor's own question on the table, whether the believer or the unbeliever is the more likely to be saved, and reading the lecture's claim that a man is more likely to be damned for believing the gospel than for rejecting it. Crrow frames why a Vatican trained clergyman with divinity credentials and several languages would say such a thing, arguing that Taylor had come to understand the institution he worshipped in, right down to who owns your birth certificate. Both treat belief as a stumbling block laid deliberately for people with real spiritual instinct."}, {"title": "Repeat A Lie And You Become One", "body": "Crrow builds a chain out of two sayings everyone already knows. The golden rule is called golden, he says, because its value outranks any other concept we can come up with, and if the truth sets you free then a liar has to be the opposite of free. From there he asks whether repeating a lie you did not know was a lie still makes you a liar, and answers yes, with no other way about it. The insidious part, he adds, is that belief is entered into by decision rather than research, and for many people it cannot be undone."}, {"title": "Talking Animals And The Old Priesthood", "body": "The conversation turns to an edict from around 680 AD ordering that Christ stop being depicted as a lamb, and Crrow carries that same strategy into the present. He compares a child sat in front of a sage teacher with a child sat in front of Sesame Street, where talking animals do the teaching, and calls the distance between them close to black magic worked under the cover of entertainment. Dylan then reads Taylor's account of how the first priests were players, exempted from common labor to watch the stars, and separates the precise year they kept from the vague year handed to everyone else."}, {"title": "Lazarus As The Dying Year", "body": "Taylor's reading of the miracle gets laid out in full. The tragedy is really the tragedy of Bethany, the house of affliction, and its meaning is the death and resurrection of the year. Lazarus is the year itself, Martha and Mary are December and January attending the dying and reviving brother, the Jews are the chorus, and the sun plays the manager who tells the audience outright that this sickness is not unto death. Crrow interjects that the priests who built these stories were burying the only moment anyone can actually live in, which is this passing second."}, {"title": "The Acceptable Year Of The Lord", "body": "Crrow tests Chance on a single word from the gospel of John, verily, and Chance ties it straight to the vernal time. The point Crrow is making is that tomorrow morning the sun will rise at the exact moment it is supposed to, without fail, which makes it the ultimate definition of truth. He then describes how a group of them went after the equinox question and found that equal day and equal night depends on your geography, so no single date can be right for everyone. Dylan calls that lost knowledge one of the most important things we have given up."}]
